Row.Text: After a long day of exploring the Babylonian capital, Dr. Rizal takes a moment to rest in the lush environs of a kirimāḫu. What a thing to have such a place in a city as large and dense as {1_Capital}, where space is precious.
The ideas that must spring from reverie here...
The water these pleasure gardens must require...

It is taking three deckhands to convince the donkey to walk into the quppu today. Perhaps, it senses a windstorm downstream. More likely, it wants a snack. The supervising tamkāru contemplates his professional options.
Long-distance trade is a trial with great return.
There are no donkeys at the lending house.

A magarru rushes across the battlefield toward a lone qašti, the charioteer intent on claiming his enemy’s head and plucking out his eyes. With haggard breath, the archer prays to Marduk the avenger and looses his arrow. A whistle, a thud, and a crash. The driver falls to the field, and the chariot staggers to a halt. Today, the qašti keeps his eyes.
Qašti are the hand of Marduk.
Thanks be to the great Avenger.

Like a theater of greenery, the gardens climb tier over tier, the highest level hosting grand trees reaching to the sky. Flowers and vines adorn the balconies, and the stone walls conceal the canals and pipes feeding the soil. Visitors from cities far distant marvel at the sight.
Beauty will be the Babylonian legacy.
Canals and machinery are the true wonder.

Two Babylonian astrologers are arguing outside the palace. One thinks the day should be divided into ten partitions, from zero to nine. The other considers the idea ludicrous. “Sixty is clearly the best number,” he states. “Zero is nothing.” Onlookers nod in agreement.

The old stele can still be seen from the grounds of {1_story_city}’s academy. Two scholars debate the importance of the laws inscribed on its surface, barely legible now but remembered clearly. Society changes as stone crumbles; perhaps laws should change too.
What is just changes with society.

Creatures from across the empire and even from neighboring regions have found a new home in the kirimāḫu. Their grace, strength, and variety provide a study in the beauty and complexity of life. Some citizens argue, however, that the greatest asset of any animal is its flesh.

As the trade caravan enters its destination, the tamkāru marvels at the city’s sights. The streets are clogged with citizens, but the visitors stand out, pointing at the wondrous constructions in awe. A hint of jealousy stabs the merchant’s heart. Babylonian cities are the fairest of all.
Trade will carry news of Babylonian marvels.

Carefully, the artisan coats bricks with a copper glaze in the shape of a lion. “Praise Ishtar, ruler of men,” he sings as he moves the coated bricks into the kiln, heating them to melt the glaze. One brick, however, is marked with a dog's paw print. The artisan scoffs and sets it aside.
Only a lion’s paw belongs on this brick.
Dogs are a divine creature as well.

Once a rich man, the sick beggar kneels before the altar. Some god has ravaged his life with evil fortune, but now, he feels life within him once more. Just a day before, his family was planning his funeral. Today, a god deserves thanks.
Thanks be to Marduk, the creator.

Sunlight sparkles off the bright bricks and tall walls in {1_story_city}. Voices ring in many languages as people jostle each other, eager to see the newest marvel of construction. In every direction, beauty; on every face, a smile.
Bricks are a medium of wonder.
Beauty is an excuse for celebration.

In the night sky, the ṭupšarrum sees the Anzû-bird’s star in the Goatfish – an omen of peace to calm the raging Pleiades. He cuts the details of the observation into the clay with his stylus, filling the final line of the fifty-third tablet.
Fetch more clay to capture the night’s remaining signs.
Rush to the court with the good news.

The young Babylonian loads up the cart with the last of his belongings. It’s his last day as a country boy; tomorrow he will be a man of the city. No longer will he spend his days tending lines of date palms under a hot sun. So much more awaits.
Engineers keep Babylon happy and fed.

The Babylonian people have spread across the land, seeming to forget the glory of ancient Babylon and its towers. Now, with steel and fired brick, one architect proposes the glorious return of the high-rise: the Tower of Bab-ilim.

The fame of the capital has spread far - would-be lords of tiny manors name their towers “Babylon” and themselves “Marduk.” Crudely-formed stone lamassu guard the entranceways to hillforts. It is fame… but is it insult?
Crack down on this - there is one Babylon, one temple of Marduk, others must be something else.
Could it be, perhaps, a franchise?
